**SUBJECT:**	A Design Project Definition for Grid Enhancement Technology: Maximizing  
Transmission Power Delivery via Dynamic Line Rating

## **INTRODUCTION: THE “STATIC” BOTTLENECK**

Traditional power transmission networks rely on conservative Static Line Ratings (SLR) that frequently restrict the integration of renewable energy by indicating system overloads. To address this bottleneck, this project aims to maximize power delivery by implementing Dynamic Line Rating (DLR) technology, which utilizes fluctuating hourly models to safely unlock previously unused grid capacity. This Project Definition establishes the team's comprehensive understanding of this engineering problem and details the ethical safety considerations, applicable IEEE standards, and operating environment specifications in this project necessary to transition to dynamic modeling. Furthermore, it summarizes the project's deliverables, which include a real-time User Interface dashboard and an accompanying economic reliability research paper. Lastly, the Project Definition will define sub-team roles for our team and management policies structured to successfully execute these objectives.

## **PROBLEM STATEMENT**

Our team’s goal is to maximize power delivered in a system. Since the Static Line Rating (SLR) uses a fixed value to ensure safety over 100% of the time, we can make a model where ratings fluctuate hourly to achieve this goal. This would utilize previously unused carrying capacity of renewable energy by implementing Dynamic Line Rating (DLR) on transmission constraints.

**Background Information**  
In traditional power systems, overhead transmission and distribution lines have a Static Line Rating (SLR). This is a fixed current limit based on "worst-case" weather assumptions, such as high ambient temperature, full solar radiation, and low wind speed. These conditions would cause the line to heat up and have lower cooling from the wind, but in general, this happens less than 5% of the time. For the other 95% of the year, especially at night or during breezy days, the line could safely carry 30–50% more power without overheating. As a consequence, we curtail cheap renewable energy because the line is technically overloaded based on the SLR, despite the physical wire actually being cool. Our team aims to not adhere to this conservative paper rating by implementing our DLR.

**Design Functionality**  
Our design will rely on software tools to utilize weather data, transmission line load data, and IEEE standard requirements to simulate real world transmission line response under given conditions to determine a Dynamic Line Rating (DLR). The goal is to design an interactable software that can intake weather data, expected load data, and relevant line specifications to output to a User Interface to showcase a more efficient DLR than the given SLR (see Figure 1 below). This application will also omit worst case scenarios. If this is more easily accomplished than anticipated and we have sufficient time, we intend to extend our design to include a device which can observe the transmission line in real time. This will then be utilized by sending all relevant data points to the software being run at the distribution center, so the DLR calculated can be effectively implemented in real transmission line systems.

### **Ethical Considerations**

Our project will adhere to the IEEE Code of Ethics, specifically regarding the safety and welfare of the public. While DLR offers efficiency, we recognize it introduces risks regarding line sag and thermal inertia. Our simulation will address this by implementing strict 'fail-safe' protocols, ensuring that if weather data becomes unreliable, the system defaults to standard static ratings to prevent catastrophic failure. Like many other engineering projects, we must balance safety and efficiency with our implementation. Right now, the SLR ensures that power lines are beyond safe.

**1\. Public Safety and Sag Risk**

We seek to utilize DLR to bypass the conservative rating to reasonably maximize power output; however, this does introduce safety risks. By removing this ‘buffer’ to push more power, you introduce physical risk, such as:

* **Clearance Violations:** As the line heats up, it physically expands and sags. If our DLR model overestimates the cooling effect of the wind, the line could sag into the environment and structures, causing flashovers, wildfires, or electrocution hazards.  
* **Weather Volatility:** Wind is volatile. If a line is loaded to 120% capacity because of the wind and it suddenly dies, the line temperature **will** spike rapidly (thermal runaway) before operators can reduce the load.

We also have risks regarding the database we would rely on, so we must also consider the following:

**2\. Data Integrity**

* **Dependency on External Data:** Our system relies on weather data (whether from sensors or NOAA). If this data stream gets interrupted, hacked, or spoofed (false data injection attack), the grid management solution could potentially overload the line believing it is cool enough to handle it.  
* **Ethical Obligation:** Engineers have an ethical duty to design "fail-safe" mechanisms. If the data cuts out, the system must default back to the conservative static rating immediately.

The applicable safety and reliability standards informing these ethical design requirements are listed in Appendix A.

### **Relevant Standards**

We will follow IEEE Standard 738 for conductor temperature and ampacity and evaluating weather conditions. We will use IEEE Standard PC37.113/D7.0 to properly plan transmission line protection for when worst-case conditions occur on our system (once we are granted access to this standard). We will follow IEEE Standard P1925.1/D1.1 for energy efficiency in dynamic line rating (once we are granted access to this standard). If we come into contact with series capacitor banks on transmission lines, we will use IEEE Standard C37.116 to ensure that we are protecting these capacitor banks correctly. We will comply with NERC Reliability Standards for transmission reliability and N-1 Contingency Criteria for contingency planning. If we are to make a hardware device to pair with our UI dashboard, then we will follow IEEE Standard 2800 for interconnecting inverter-based resources with transmission systems (Full descriptions of all applicable standards are provided in Appendix A).

### **Project Deliverables**

Since the methodology for evaluating conditions determining line limits is the main basis for originality in our project, our team has yet to determine what that system will look like. We plan to make a UI dashboard for this evaluation system and a research paper to prove the economic and reliability benefits for SLR versus DLR. Our team has also considered making a hardware component that links with the UI dashboard if time permits, but we are committed to the two deliverables mentioned before.

**UI Specifications**  
We plan to develop a UI dashboard that provides a centralized interface for monitoring real-time line conditions, visualizing dynamic capacity, and forecast future ratings based on environmental inputs. The dashboard should follow established safety standards for human-machine interfaces (HMIs), as well as ISO 9241, which emphasizes guidance for clear, consistent, and readable design.

The application should also align with IEEE Std 2030.2 (Guide for the Interoperability of Energy Storage Systems with the Electric Power Infrastructure) for guidance on monitoring interfaces, IEEE Std 1815 for ensuring robust communication protocols between the dashboard and telemetry devices, and IEEE Std C37.118 for synchrophasor measurement between power systems (see Appendix A for full standard descriptions).

We made a mock-up UI dashboard shown below. Currently, we plan for users to only be able to select from a preset amount of locations that are in our database. Then, using the database, the program will calculate a new dynamic thermal limit and the duration it should be trusted for. The dashboard will also show the current sag of the line and the current weather condition.

**Operating Environment Specifications**  
The operating environment for this Dynamic Line Rating (DLR) system encompasses both the physical atmospheric conditions affecting the bare overhead conductors and the computational infrastructure hosting the software application.

Physically, the transmission lines operate in dynamic outdoor environments subject to continuous weather fluctuations. The system must accurately model thermal responses across a wide spectrum of atmospheric variables, rather than relying solely on the static worst-case assumptions of 40°C ambient temperatures, full solar radiation, and minimal 0.6 m/s wind speeds. The design will utilize IEEE Standard 738 (see Appendix A for full standard descriptions) to evaluate these varied weather conditions and continuously calculate the safe conductor temperature and ampacity relationships.

Computationally, the DLR software and user interface dashboard will be operated centrally at a distribution center. The software environment requires a stable network connection to ingest continuous external weather data streams from sensors or NOAA. The underlying analysis will be supported by power system simulation platforms, such as PSSE or EMTP, to evaluate grid reliability. Additionally, the environment will utilize data processing pipelines, such as built in data analysis environments like Python or Jupyter Notebooks, to preprocess incoming datasets, execute the forecasting machine learning models, and feed the UI dashboard.

**Performance Specifications**  
To understand if our solution of DLR is functioning, we will implement contingency checking, defined as analyses of a system composed of N active components where, given the failure of one component, the other N-1 components can be adjusted to compensate for the missing load. Our DLR methodology will implement this to ensure that for a given power grid, there are sufficient failsafes to prevent system failure. The standards outlining what these analyses entail are detailed in Appendix A.

**Input/Output Specifications**  
The following table outlines the inputs and outputs for our system:

| Location (I) | Ambient Temperature (I) \[°C\] | Wind Speed (I) \[m/s\] | Solar Irradiance (I) \[W/m^2\] | Worst Case Static Limit (I) \[A\] | New Thermal Limit (O) \[A\] | Trusted Duration of New Limit (O) \[s\] |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Austin** | **\-5.50 to 41.70** | **0.20 to 8.00** | **0.00 to 563.00** | **800-3000** | **800-4500** | **10** |
| **Corpus Christi** | **1.40 to 37.10** | **0.30 to 12.10** | **0.00 to 579.00** | **1000-5000** | **1000-7500** | **10** |
| **Midland** | **\-9.40 to 43.80** | **0.20 to 11.70** | **0.00 to 574.00** | **600-3000** | **600-4500** | **10** |
| **El Paso** | **\-5.10 to 41.40** | **0.20 to 13.50** | **0.00 to 533.00** | **600-2300** | **600-3450** | **20** |

The provided input/output specification table delineates the environmental and operational boundaries for a Dynamic Line Rating (DLR) system across four Texas cities: Austin, Corpus Christi, Midland, and El Paso. The "Inputs" (I) capture the fluctuating atmospheric variables—ambient temperature, wind speed, and solar irradiance—alongside the traditional "Worst Case" Static Line Ratings (SLR) that currently govern these grids. The "Outputs" (O) define the new calculated thermal limits in Amperes and the "Trusted Duration," which specifies the window of time (either 10 or 20 seconds) that these higher dynamic limits can be safely maintained before the system requires a data refresh.

The primary purpose of this table is to quantify the "Static Bottleneck" by showing the potential delta between conservative paper ratings and real-time physical capacity. By defining these ranges, the project team can develop software models that transition from worst-case assumptions to time-varying ampacity that reflects actual cooling conditions. This structured data serves as the foundation for the UI dashboard and machine learning models, ensuring the system can safely unlock up to 30-50% more power delivery while adhering to fail-safe protocols if data integrity is compromised.

**TEAM ORGANIZATION**  
**Project Roles**  
The Data Science Team is responsible for collection, processing, and analysis of weather and grid data to preprocess input datasets. They will work on quantifying the statistical and economical benefits of Dynamic Line Rating and developing an ML model to forecast maximum line throughput based on external conditions. The Power Systems Team is responsible for evaluating grid reliability and N-1 contingency performance under dynamic versus static line ratings. The Software Team is responsible for implementing software-based UI design to monitor, forecast, and adjust dynamic line rating at the grid level, which includes visualizations and automated outputs.

**Team Policies**  
For our project, we will be using Github for code collaboration, PSSE for grid simulation, Discord, and GDrive for communication and organization.

Our team expectations are to be present at weekly meetings with TA on Wednesday, Bi-weekly meetings with faculty mentor on Monday, and weekly team progress checks on Friday. We will self-assign goals in project documentation, communicating if deadlines are missed or issues arise to adjust accordingly.

Our team has established a structured approach to conflict resolution and decision-making to ensure smooth collaboration throughout the project. For decision-making, we use a tiered approach: significant decisions regarding project scope, steps for moving forward, or deliverable viability are discussed with our faculty mentor during our bi-weekly meetings; decisions that affect the entire team and project, such as design pivots or scope changes, are addressed during our weekly check-ins and work sessions and require team consensus; and for everyday decisions, the person most responsible for that task decides.

For design disagreements, we aim to focus on evaluating ideas and ensuring everyone understands competing proposals clearly before discussion. We then evaluate each option against agreed-upon or required criteria rather than personal preference, and after the conflict is concluded, we document the decision and reasoning for future reference. For interpersonal conflict, team members are responsible for addressing tension directly and early in private, where both parties must allow the other to express their perspective, refrain from accusations, and aim to acquire mutual understanding. If they are unable to resolve the issue privately, a neutral team member or advisor will be brought in to facilitate.

To address poor behavior or performance issues, we first reference the responsibilities and deliverables established at the beginning of our project to create a baseline for expectations. If performance issues arise, we begin with a private and non-accusatory conversation to understand the causes, such as personal stress, large workload, or confusion about tasks, and find ways to help, such as splitting work into smaller parts or redistributing tasks. If the issue continues, the full team will be made aware to resolve the problem, create a plan to implement changes that are doable for all, and document agreed changes. Finally, if the problem persists and affects project progress, we will escalate to our faculty advisor with documentation.

## **CONCLUSION**

This project investigates the feasibility of Dynamic Line Rating as a method for improving the operational efficiency of existing transmission infrastructure by replacing conservative Static Line Ratings with time-varying ampacity calculated from environmental conditions. As traditional Static Line Ratings are built on worst-case weather assumptions that occur less than 5% of the time, the remaining 95% of operating hours represent significant untapped capacity.

To overcome the inefficiencies caused by worst-case static assumptions, our team seeks to demonstrate through simulation and research that existing transmission lines can safely carry substantially more power when ratings are informed by real-time conditions rather than fixed assumptions. Our approach combines weather and grid data analysis, IEEE 738-based ampacity modeling, and N-1 contingency evaluation to ensure reliability and public safety (see Appendix A). Fail-safe protocols will ensure the system defaults to static ratings whenever data integrity is compromised, maintaining the ethical standard of engineering.

The deliverables for this project include a Dynamic Line Rating simulation, a UI dashboard for real-time monitoring and dynamic rating visualization, and a research paper quantifying the economic and reliability benefits of DLR. Through our deliverables, we seek to provide both a practical tool and an academic contribution to the field. By assessing whether operational awareness and modeling can unlock additional capacity from existing infrastructure, this project offers insight into the viability of Dynamic Line Rating as a reliable, cost-effective solution to growing electricity consumption in the 21st century.

**APPENDIX A: APPLICABLE STANDARDS**

1. **IEEE Standard 738 \- Standard for Calculating the Current-Temperature Relationship of Bare Overhead Conductors**  
   A numerical method by which the core and surface temperatures of a bare overhead conductor are related to the steady or time-varying electrical current and weather conditions is described in this standard. Contents discussed also include how this method may be used to determine the conductor’s current for a corresponding conductor temperature limit. Please note the content in this standard does not recommend suitable weather conditions or conductor parameters for use in line rating calculations \[4\].  
2. **IEEE Standard PC37.113/D7.0 \- Guide for Protective Relay Applications to Transmission Lines**   
   Information on the concepts of protection of AC transmission lines is presented in this standard. Applications of the concepts to accepted transmission line protection schemes are presented as well. Many important issues, such as coordination of settings, operating times, characteristics of relays, mutual coupling of lines, automatic reclosing, use of communication channels, are examined. Special protection systems, protection of multi-terminal lines and single-phase tripping and reclosing are also included. The impact of different electrical parameters and system performance considerations on the selection of relays and protection schemes is discussed as well. The purpose of this guide is to provide a reference for the selection of relay schemes and to assist less experienced protective relaying engineers in applying protection schemes to transmission lines \[5\].  
3. **IEEE Standard P1925.1/D1.1 \- Guide for Energy Efficiency in Dynamic Line Rating Systems**  
   This standard specifies an energy-efficient, rate 1 and modulation adaptive transmission system designed for the deployment of mixed line rates in optical networks. It introduces the transmission system and provides mechanisms to optimally configure the line rate to efficiently accommodate varying traffic loads while reducing the power consumption \[6\].  
4. **IEEE Standard C37.116 \- Guide for Protective Relay Applications to Transmission Lines Series Capacitor Banks**  
   The application of protective relays on transmission-line series capacitor banks is covered. Ample discussion of the protection and control issues related to series capacitor bank installations is provided to the reader. Specific examples related to protective functions and testing procedures are provided \[7\].  
5. **IEEE Standard 2800 \- Standard for Interconnection and Interoperability of Inverter-Based Resources with Associated Transmission Electric Power Systems**  
   Uniform technical minimum requirements for the interconnection, capability, and lifetime performance of inverter-based resources interconnecting with transmission and sub-transmission systems are established in this standard. Included in this standard are performance requirements for reliable integration of inverter-based resources into the bulk power system, including, but not limited to, voltage and frequency ride-through, active power control, reactive power control, dynamic active power support under abnormal frequency conditions, dynamic voltage support under abnormal voltage conditions, power quality, and negative sequence current injection \[8\].  
6. **IEEE Standard 2030.2 \- Guide for the Interoperability of Energy Storage Systems Integrated with the Electric Power Infrastructure**  
   Application of this standard includes: (1) Stationary battery energy storage system (BESS) and mobile BESS; (2) Carrier of BESS, including but not limited to lead acid battery, lithium ion battery, flow battery, and sodium-sulfur battery; (3) BESS used in electric power systems (EPS). Also provided in this standard are alternatives for connection (including DR interconnection), design, operation, and maintenance of stationary or mobile BESS used in EPS. Introduction, overview, and engineering issues related to the BESS are given \[9\].  
7. **IEEE Standard 1815 \- Standard for Electric Power Systems Communications \- Distributed Network Protocol (DNP3)**  
   This document specifies the standard approach for mapping between IEEE Std 1815™ \[Distributed Network Protocol (DNP3)\] and IEC 61850 (Communications Networks and Systems for Power Utility Automation). Two primary use cases are addressed: a) mapping between an IEEE 1815-based master and an IEC 61850-based remote site and b) mapping between an IEC 61850-based master and an IEEE 1815-based remote site. Mapping aspects included in the standard are: conceptual architecture; general mapping requirements; the mapping of Common Data Classes, Constructed Attribute Classes and Abstract Communication Service Interface (ACSI); cyber security requirements, the architecture of a gateway used for translation and requirements for embedding mapping configuration information into IEC 61850 System Configuration Description Language (SCL) and DNP3 Device Profile. This standard addresses a selection of features, data classes, and services of the two standards \[10\].  
8. **IEEE Standard C37.118 \- Standard for Synchrophasor Measurements for Power Systems**  
   IEEE C37.118 establishes measurement definitions and compliance requirements for synchrophasor measurements, frequency, and rate of change of frequency (ROCOF) under varying power systems operating conditions. It specifies time synchronization and accuracy requirements, which are critical for ensuring that real-time data fed into the DLR system reflects true line conditions \[11\].  
9. **NERC Reliability Standards \- North American Electric Reliability Corporation**  
   NERC Reliability Standards establish mandatory requirements for the planning the operation of the bulk electric power system across North America. This project complies with NERC standards to ensure that the DLR simulation meets transmission reliability requirements, including contingency planning criteria that govern how the system must perform under abnormal operation conditions \[12\].   
10. **N-1 Contingency Criteria**  
    The N-1 Contingency Criterion requires that the bulk power system remain within thermal, voltage, and stability limits following the sudden loss of any single system component. The Power Systems team will evaluate whether transmission lines operating under dynamic ratings satisfy N-1 criteria, ensuring redistributed loads can be safely absorbed without violating limits or compromising system reliability \[13\].  
11. **ISO 9241 \- Ergonomics of Human-System Interaction**  
    ISO 9241 establishes “requirements and recommendations for human-centered design principles applied throughout the development lifecycles of interactive computer-based systems.” For this project, it guides the design of the UI dashboard to ensure that grid operators can efficiently interpret dynamic line rating data and navigate system alerts. By following this standard, the dashboard will prioritize clarity, consistency, and usability, reducing the likelihood of operator error in time-sensitive situations \[14\].
